analysis.one_liner: Ends required private mortgage insurance once homeowners build enough equity, with automatic termination and refunds.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 421-7 and the Senate passed it by unanimous consent, and it became the Homeowners Protection Act of 1998.
analysis.plain_summary: When a homebuyer puts down less than 20 percent, the lender usually requires private mortgage insurance, and borrowers historically kept paying it long after they had built enough equity. This bill lets borrowers cancel the insurance when their loan balance reaches 80 percent of the home's original value, forces it to end automatically at 78 percent, requires clear annual notices about these rights, and requires refunds of unearned premiums. A Senate-added housing title also extended flood insurance and federal housing programs, added disclosure rules for reverse mortgages sold to seniors, and abolished a leftover federal oversight board.
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers who put less than 20 percent down and were required to pay private mortgage insurance. They gain the right to cancel the insurance in writing at 80 percent loan-to-value, automatic termination at 78 percent, annual statements telling them these rights exist, refunds of unearned premiums within 45 days, and legal recourse against servicers or insurers that keep charging. A separate title adds disclosure rules so seniors taking reverse mortgages are told all costs and cannot be made to fund unnecessary or excessive fees.

how_it_helps.text: Borrowers can cancel private mortgage insurance by written request once their balance reaches 80 percent of the home's original value, if they have a good payment history [S5].
The insurance requirement ends automatically at 78 percent of original value for borrowers who are current on payments, with unearned premiums returned within 45 days [S5].
Lenders must disclose at closing and in annual statements when the insurance can be canceled or terminates, and cannot charge any fee for these disclosures [S5].
The rules override conflicting servicing agreements with Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and private investors, and supersede weaker state laws while leaving stronger state termination rules in place [S5].

A Senate-added title requires full disclosure of all costs in home equity conversion mortgages for seniors and lets HUD bar funding of unnecessary or excessive estate-planning or advice fees [S4][S5].

analysis.who_pays: Private mortgage insurers lose premiums they previously collected for years after borrowers had built real equity. Lenders and servicers bear the cost of new disclosures, annual notices, tracking termination dates, and refunding unearned premiums, and servicers that violate the rules face civil damages up to statutory caps.

drawbacks.text: Lender-paid mortgage insurance is excluded from all cancellation and termination rights; borrowers steered into it pay through a higher interest rate for the life of the loan and only get a notice suggesting they review refinancing options [S5].

Lenders can exempt loans they deem high-risk from the cancellation and automatic termination rules, extending them until the midpoint of the loan's amortization period, which for a 30-year loan is year 15 [S5].
Mortgages made before the law took effect only get annual notices about possible cancellation rights, not automatic termination, so existing borrowers gain far less than new ones [S5].

Liability is capped and limited: servicers are not liable for a mortgage insurer's or lender's failure to comply, and class action recoveries are capped at the lesser of $500,000 or 1 percent of net worth [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a well-designed consumer win with real, modest limits. It ended a widespread practice in which borrowers paid insurance premiums long after they were warranted, and it did so with clear dates, mandatory notices, and refunds rather than vague standards. The main gaps are that lender-paid insurance slips through untouched, high-risk loans get a weaker standard, and pre-existing mortgages get only notices.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it nearly unanimously, the Senate added a package of housing provisions and passed it by unanimous consent, and the House agreed to the Senate version in 1998, making it the Homeowners Protection Act of 1998.

narrative.text: Rep. James V. Hansen introduced the bill on February 5, 1997, originally requiring only disclosure of private mortgage insurance cancellation rights [S1][S2][S7].

The House Banking and Financial Services Committee reported it as amended on a 36-1 vote, and the strengthened version added mandatory termination of private mortgage insurance by operation of law [S3][S7].
The House passed the bill 421-7 on April 16, 1997, under a procedure requiring a two-thirds majority, with 202 of 205 Democrats and 218 of 226 Republicans voting yes [S7][S8].
On November 13, 1997, the Senate passed the bill with an amendment by unanimous consent; Senator Lott proposed the amendment on behalf of Senator D'Amato [S4][S7].

The Senate-added package extended federal housing programs through FY 1998-1999, added senior reverse mortgage protections, and abolished the Thrift Depositor Protection Oversight Board, alongside the Homeowners Protection Act title [S4][S5].
The bill became law in 1998 as the Homeowners Protection Act of 1998 (Public Law 105-216) [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Homebuyers with small down payments are better off: they keep hundreds of dollars a year once their equity reaches roughly 20 percent, rather than paying mortgage insurers indefinitely. Mortgage insurers and lenders lose the premium revenue the old rules let them keep.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was overwhelming and bipartisan: 202 of 205 Democrats and 218 of 226 Republicans voted yes in the House, and the Senate passed it by unanimous consent; the 33 original cosponsors included 12 Republicans and 21 Democrats [S6][S8].

industries.note: Their business depends on borrowers paying premiums after equity passes 20 percent; the bill forces cancellation at 80 percent and automatic termination at 78 percent, cutting off that tail of revenue. Borrowers' savings come directly out of premium income.

They lose fee and premium flow tied to prolonged mortgage insurance and take on disclosure, notice, and refund duties. But the bill limits their liability, guarantees they need not repurchase loans when they cancel PMI in compliance, and preempts conflicting investor servicing agreements [S5].

industries.industry: Reverse mortgage lenders and estate-planning or advisory services marketed to seniors
industries.note: A Senate-added title requires full disclosure of all costs in home equity conversion mortgages and lets HUD restrict seniors from funding unnecessary or excessive estate-planning or advice costs through the mortgage [S4][S5].
